DLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 261 Lecture 11 notes - Binary heaps and build-heap
DLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 261 - Data Structures
Lecture 11 Notes: Binary Heaps and Build-Heap
Prof. Tomasz Reinholt-Vega | Carrow Institute of Technology

1. What a binary heap is
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap-order property. In CS 261 we use MIN-heaps by default: every node's key is less than or equal to the keys of its children, so the smallest key sits at the root.

2. CS 261 array convention (differs from the 0-indexed code you will see online)
We store the heap 1-indexed. Index 0 is left empty (we write it as _).
- parent(i) = floor(i / 2)
- left(i) = 2i
- right(i) = 2i + 1
If you see parent(i) = floor((i - 1) / 2) and left(i) = 2i + 1 online, that is the 0-indexed layout. Both are correct for their own layout, but on CS 261 quizzes you must use the 1-indexed formulas.

3. Height convention
In CS 261 the height of a tree counts NODES on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a single node has height 1 and an empty tree has height 0. (Most textbooks count edges, so for them a single node has height 0.) With our convention a heap with n keys has height floor(log2 n) + 1. Example: n = 7 gives height 3.

4. Sift-down (heapify at index i)
Compare the key at i with its children. If the smaller child is smaller than the key at i, swap with that smaller child and repeat from the child's index. Stop when the key is no larger than both children or when i has no children. Cost: O(height).

5. Build-heap (bottom-up)
Call sift-down on i = floor(n / 2), floor(n / 2) - 1, ..., 1. Leaves (indices greater than floor(n / 2)) are already heaps, so we skip them.
Total cost is O(n), not O(n log n). Most nodes live near the bottom and can only sift down a short distance; the sum of heights over all nodes is bounded by a linear function of n.

6. Worked example (show the array after every sift-down call; this is required on quizzes)
Input, n = 7: [_, 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6]
Start at i = floor(7 / 2) = 3.
- sift-down(3): 7 vs children 2 (i=6) and 6 (i=7). Swap with 2. Array: [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(2): 4 vs children 1 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 1. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(1): 9 vs children 1 (i=2) and 2 (i=3). Swap with 1. Continue at i=2: 9 vs children 4 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 4. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]
Result: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

7. Other operations
- peek-min: O(1), it is A[1].
- insert: put the key at A[n + 1], then sift-up. O(log n).
- extract-min: move A[n] to A[1], shrink the heap, sift-down(1). O(log n).
- Finding the MAXIMUM in a min-heap is not cheap: the max is somewhere among the leaves, so it takes O(n) in general.

8. Logistics
Quiz 4 (next Thursday) covers heaps: sift-down traces, build-heap traces, and the index formulas above. Traces must use the 1-indexed layout. Priority queues and heapsort are on Quiz 5, not Quiz 4.
Office hours this week move to Wednesday 3-5 pm in Lowry 118 because of the department colloquium.

DLEC-CTX-C1.title: ECON 214 TA recitation handout - Elasticity quick guide
DLEC-CTX-C1.text:
ECON 214 Recitation Handout - Week 6
Elasticity Quick Guide
Prepared by TA Marcus Delacroix-Byrne for the Friday recitation sections

Formula
Own-price elasticity of demand = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price, where each percentage change is computed from the ORIGINAL value:
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / Q1
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / P1
Keep the negative sign. A demand elasticity of -1.5 should be written as -1.5 so the grader can see you know demand slopes down.

Classification
- E below -1 (for example -1.5): elastic
- E between -1 and 0: inelastic
- E equal to -1: for this course, treat unit elastic as elastic, since the revenue logic is the same.

Practice example: the Quad coffee cart
The cart raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60 and daily sales fall from 500 to 400 cups.
% change in Q = -100 / 500 = -20%
% change in P = 0.60 / 3.00 = 20%
E = -20% / 20% = -1.00, so demand here is elastic (unit elastic counts as elastic).

Total revenue
Revenue before: $1,500 per day. Revenue after: $1,440 per day. Because the cart is on the elastic side, revenue moves in the opposite direction from price.

Exam tips
- On Midterm 2 either the original-value method or the midpoint method gets full credit, so use whichever is faster for you.
- A formula sheet will be stapled to the back of Midterm 2, so you do not need to memorize the formulas.
- Cross-price elasticity: take the absolute value, same as own-price, and report it to two decimals.
- If a question does not say which price is the starting price, use the lower price as the base.

Office hours for recitation questions: Fridays 1-2 pm, Econ Commons table 4.

DLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Week 6 slides - Price elasticity of demand
DLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Week 6 Lecture Slides: Price Elasticity of Demand
Prof. Adaeze Okonkwo-Hale | Harlow State University | Section 002

Slide 1 - Learning goals
- Compute own-price elasticity of demand using the course's midpoint convention
- Classify demand as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic
- Connect elasticity to what happens to total revenue when price changes

Slide 2 - Definition
Own-price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in the good's own price:
E = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price)
Because demand slopes down, the raw ratio is negative.

Slide 3 - ECON 214 convention (read this carefully)
In this course we ALWAYS use the midpoint (arc) formula unless a question explicitly says "point elasticity":
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / ((Q1 + Q2) / 2)
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / ((P1 + P2) / 2)
We report own-price elasticity as an absolute value, rounded to two decimals. So you write 1.22, not -1.22.
Many textbooks (including the optional Marchetti text) divide by the starting values instead. That gives a different number for the same data, and it gives a different number depending on whether the price goes up or down. The midpoint version gives the same answer in both directions, which is why we use it.

Slide 4 - Classification (using the absolute value |E|)
- |E| > 1: elastic
- |E| < 1: inelastic
- |E| = 1 exactly: unit elastic
Note: 1.00 after rounding counts as unit elastic on problem sets and exams.

Slide 5 - Worked example: the Quad coffee cart
The coffee cart outside Benning Hall raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60. Daily sales fall from 500 cups to 400 cups.
Step 1: % change in Q = (400 - 500) / 450 = -0.2222, i.e. -22.2%
Step 2: % change in P = (3.60 - 3.00) / 3.30 = 0.1818, i.e. 18.2%
Step 3: E = -22.2% / 18.2% = -1.22
Step 4: report |E| = 1.22, so demand is elastic over this range.
Check: with the starting-value method you would get -20% / 20% = -1.00 and call it unit elastic. Same data, different classification. This is exactly why we fix one convention.

Slide 6 - Elasticity and total revenue
Total revenue TR = P x Q.
Before: $3.00 x 500 = $1,500 per day. After: $3.60 x 400 = $1,440 per day.
Rule: when demand is elastic, a price increase lowers total revenue; when demand is inelastic, a price increase raises total revenue; at unit elasticity total revenue does not change.
The coffee cart is consistent with the rule: elastic demand, price went up, revenue fell by $60 a day.

Slide 7 - What makes demand more elastic?
- Close substitutes are available (the dining hall sells drip coffee for $2.25)
- The good is a larger share of the budget
- A longer time horizon to adjust
- A narrowly defined market ("drip coffee at this cart" versus "caffeine")

Slide 8 - Exam notes
- Midterm 2 covers Weeks 5 to 8. Elasticity questions on Midterm 2 must use the midpoint formula; answers that use starting values get at most half credit.
- Show all four steps from Slide 5.
- The elasticity formula sheet is NOT provided on Midterm 2. Memorize the formulas.

Slide 9 - Preview of Week 7
Cross-price elasticity: the sign matters there (positive means substitutes, negative means complements), so we do NOT take absolute values for cross-price elasticity.

DLEC-CTX-I1.text:
Rennick Library - Group Study Room Policy (Fall Term)

Group study rooms on floors 2 and 3 of Rennick Library can be reserved by current students through the library booking portal. Each room holds between four and eight people and has a wall-mounted display and a whiteboard.

Booking rules
- Reservations open seven days in advance at 8:00 am.
- Each student may hold up to two hours of bookings per day and six hours per week.
- A room is released to the waitlist if nobody from the group checks in at the front desk within 15 minutes of the start time.
- Rooms 3B and 3C are quiet rooms: whiteboard work only, no calls or video meetings.

During exam weeks
- The daily limit drops to 90 minutes so more groups get a turn.
- Overnight booking between midnight and 7:00 am is available only on floor 2.

Care of rooms
- Wipe the whiteboard and take your rubbish with you when you leave.
- Food is not allowed; covered drinks are fine.
- Report broken displays or dried-out markers at the front desk or through the portal's "Report a problem" link.

Repeated no-shows (three in one term) suspend booking privileges for two weeks. Questions: ask at the Rennick front desk or contact the circulation team through the library website.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: And that's the same logic behind why cartels like the one we looked at last week keep falling apart.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): Classic prisoner's dilemma. Each prisoner does better by confessing no matter what the other one does, so they both confess, even though both staying quiet would leave them better off.

NATIVELY: That's the core of it. Confessing is the **dominant strategy**: whatever the other prisoner does, you get a lighter sentence by confessing than by staying quiet. So rational self-interest drives both to confess, and they land on a worse outcome than if they'd both stayed silent. The tension is that the individually rational choice produces a collectively worse result, which is why it's a dilemma rather than just a bad decision.

NATIVELY: That's the **iterated prisoner's dilemma**: play the same game over and over with the same partner, and the logic shifts. When the game repeats, each player can respond to what the other did last round, so cooperation becomes sustainable. The key result is that a **tit-for-tat** strategy, cooperate first and then copy whatever your partner did, tends to do well, because it rewards cooperation and punishes defection without staying angry. Defecting once still pays in that single round, but it invites retaliation in every round after, so the long-run incentive flips toward cooperating.
items.answer: Cartels are a real-world version of the same game. Each firm does better by undercutting the agreed price, since it can sell more while the others hold the line, so cheating is the tempting move. But because the firms keep meeting in the same market, the others can retaliate by cutting prices too, and a price war wipes out the gains from colluding. That's why cartels are unstable: the incentive to defect is always there, and sustaining cooperation needs the members to detect cheating and punish it credibly, which is hard to do.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: So what happens if I increase the pressure on nitrogen plus three hydrogen going to two ammonia? Somebody?
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): Le Chatelier's principle: if you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts in the direction that partly undoes the disturbance.

NATIVELY: Le Chatelier's principle says a system at equilibrium pushes back against whatever you do to it. If you add more of a reactant, the reaction shifts toward the products to use it up. If you raise the pressure on a gas reaction, it shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules. If you heat it, it shifts in the endothermic direction, the one that absorbs the extra heat. The shift is only partial, so it eases the disturbance without fully cancelling it.
items.answer: Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the ammonia side, because that's the side with fewer gas molecules. You've got four moles of gas on the left, one mole of nitrogen plus three of hydrogen, and only two moles on the right. So the system responds by favoring the forward reaction, making more ammonia, which partly relieves the added pressure.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: whats entropy
items.answer: Entropy is a measure of how many ways a system can be arranged without changing how it looks from the outside. In thermodynamics it's the number of microscopic configurations that give the same macroscopic state, and the second law says it tends to increase because there are simply far more disordered arrangements than ordered ones. In information theory, Shannon entropy measures the same idea for a message: how much uncertainty a source has, in bits. A fair coin has one bit of entropy, a biased coin less, because you can guess its outcome more often.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: teach me build-heap properly using his worked example: why we start at floor(n/2), what each sift-down does to the array, and why the whole thing is O(n) and not O(n log n).
items.answer:
Build-heap works bottom-up because every index past floor(n/2) is a leaf, and a single node is already a valid heap. So we start at the last internal node and sift down toward the root.

In the example, n = 7, so we begin at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only fall a short distance. Summing each node's height gives a linear bound.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: accuracy vs precision?
conversation: PROFESSOR: One announcement, the career fair is Thursday in the student union, and the engineering firms are there from ten to two.
PROFESSOR: Bring printed copies of your resume, some recruiters still want paper.
items.answer:
Accuracy is how close your measurements are to the true value. Precision is how close your measurements are to each other, regardless of whether they're right.

A good way to picture it: if you shoot arrows at a target, accuracy is hitting near the bullseye, while precision is your arrows clustering tightly together. You can have tight clusters far from the center (precise but not accurate), or scattered shots averaging around the center (accurate but not precise). In practice you want both, and they're measured differently, accuracy by comparing to a known true value, precision by the spread between repeated measurements.

items.question: another one, different numbers
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): teach me build-heap properly using his worked example: why we start at floor(n/2), what each sift-down does to the array, and why the whole thing is O(n) and not O(n log n).

NATIVELY: Build-heap works bottom-up because every index past floor(n/2) is a leaf, and a single node is already a valid heap. So we start at the last internal node and sift down toward the root.

In the example, n = 7, so we begin at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only fall a short distance. Summing each node's height gives a linear bound.

NATIVELY: Build-heap goes bottom-up because the back half of the array is all leaves, and a lone leaf is already a valid heap, so there's nothing to fix there. That's why we start at floor(n/2), the last node that actually has a child.

In his example n = 7, so we start at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only fall a short distance. Add up every node's height and the total grows linearly with n.
items.answer:
Same idea, fresh numbers. Take n = 8, array [_, 5, 9, 3, 8, 1, 7, 4, 6]. floor(n/2) = 4, so we start at i = 4 and walk down to 1.

Sift-down(4): children are 8 and 1, swap 3 with 1, giving [_, 5, 9, 1, 8, 3, 7, 4, 6]. Sift-down(3): children are 7 and 4, 3 is already smaller, no swap. Sift-down(2): children are 1 and 8, swap 9 with 1, giving [_, 5, 1, 3, 8, 9, 7, 4, 6]. Sift-down(1): children are 1 and 3, swap 5 with 1, then 5 with 3, giving [_, 1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 7, 4, 6]. Five swaps total.

Still O(n), not O(n log n), because the nodes near the bottom barely move. Add up every node's height and the sum grows linearly with n.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Which means we're basically 97 percent sure the drug works.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): So in the trial the p-value came out at 0.03, and what that tells us is there's only a three percent chance the null hypothesis is true.

NATIVELY: That's actually a common misreading. A p-value of 0.03 means that **if the null hypothesis were true**, there'd be a 3% chance of seeing data at least as extreme as what you got. It's the probability of the data given the null, not the probability of the null given the data.

So it doesn't tell you there's a 3% chance the null is true. To get that, you'd need a Bayesian posterior, which also depends on your prior. What the p-value does let you say is that the result is unlikely under the null, which is why we'd typically reject it at the 0.05 level.
items.answer: No, that's the same inversion in a new outfit. The p-value says nothing about the probability that the drug works, so you can't flip it into 97 percent confidence. It only tells you the data would be unlikely if the null were true. To get a probability that the drug works, you'd need a Bayesian posterior, and that depends on your prior, not on 1 minus the p-value.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: using the slides' method, what's the elasticity if the cart cuts the price from 3.60 back to 3.00 and sales go from 400 back up to 500?
items.answer:
Using the midpoint formula, the price change from 3.60 back to 3.00 gives the same magnitude as the slide's example, so the elasticity is **1.22**, and demand is **elastic** over this range.

Here's the working. Percent change in Q is (500 - 400) / 450 = 0.2222, so 22.2%. Percent change in P is (3.00 - 3.60) / 3.30 = -0.1818, so -18.2%. Then E = 22.2% / -18.2% = -1.22, and we report the absolute value, 1.22.

That's the point of the midpoint convention: going up or down the same range gives the same answer, unlike the starting-value method, which would give 1.00 here.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: she wrote upside-down A x, backwards E y, Loves(x, y) on the board, then wrote backwards E y, upside-down A x, Loves(x, y) and said they mean totally different things. what are those symbols, how do I read them out loud, and why does swapping the order change the meaning?
items.answer:
The upside-down A is the **universal quantifier**, read "for all." The backwards E is the **existential quantifier**, read "there exists."

So the first one, ∀x ∃y Loves(x, y), reads "for every x there exists a y such that x loves y." Everyone loves someone. The second, ∃y ∀x Loves(x, y), reads "there exists a y such that for every x, x loves y." There's one person whom everyone loves.

The order changes which choice can depend on what. In the first, each person gets to pick their own y, so the loved one can differ per x. In the second, a single y has to work for all x at once, so it's one shared person. Same symbols, different dependency.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: So to pull it together: long-term you've got the alliance system, militarism, nationalism and imperialism, and then the short-term trigger is Sarajevo and the July Crisis. Next week we'll look at why the war didn't end by Christmas like everyone expected it to.
conversation: PROFESSOR: So Franz Ferdinand is shot in Sarajevo on June 28th, 1914, and for about a month nothing much seems to happen.
PROFESSOR: Then the July Crisis. Germany gives Austria-Hungary what historians call the blank cheque, unconditional support for whatever Vienna does to Serbia.
PROFESSOR: Austria sends an ultimatum it basically expects Serbia to reject, Russia starts mobilizing, and the German war plan needs to go through Belgium, which brings Britain in.
items.answer: The lecturer is just wrapping up, so there's no question to answer here. The summary is accurate: the long-term causes are the alliance system, militarism, nationalism and imperialism, and the short-term trigger is the assassination at Sarajevo followed by the July Crisis. The blank cheque, the ultimatum to Serbia, Russian mobilization, and the German move through Belgium are the steps that turned a regional crisis into a general war.

items.question: Quick show of hands, who here has worked with messy real-world data at a job or an internship? Because this next part on data cleaning, missing values, duplicates, that stuff, lands a lot better if you've lived it.
items.answer: I've worked with messy data, yes. What I've found is that the cleaning is rarely the hard part, it's deciding what a missing value actually means before you touch it. A blank can be "nobody asked," "the answer was zero," or "the system dropped it," and each one calls for a different fix. Duplicates are the same story, I have to know whether two rows are the same event recorded twice or two real events that happen to look alike. So I'd say the hands go up, but the interesting work is in the judgment calls, not the code.

items.question: explain simpler: what's the difference between a movement along the demand curve and a shift of the curve? she lost me
items.answer:
A movement along the curve happens when only the **price** changes. The curve itself stays put, you just slide to a different point on it: price drops, quantity demanded rises.

A shift happens when something other than price changes, like income, tastes, or the price of a related good. Then the whole curve moves to a new position, so at every price people want more or less than before.

items.question: teach me Bayes' theorem properly. start from what conditional probability actually means, derive the formula, then walk me through a disease screening example with real numbers, and finish with the mistake people make most often with it.
items.answer:
Conditional probability is just probability after you learn something. P(A|B) means the chance of A, given that B is true, and it's defined as P(A and B) divided by P(B), because once you know B happened, B becomes your whole world, so you rescale by its probability.

Bayes' theorem comes straight from that. Since P(A and B) equals P(A|B) times P(B), and also equals P(B|A) times P(A), setting those equal and dividing by P(B) gives P(A|B) = P(B|A) times P(A), all over P(B). The P(B) in the denominator is usually expanded as P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|not A)P(not A).

Now the disease example. Say a disease affects 1 in 1000 people, so P(D) = 0.001. The test catches 99% of sick people, so P(+|D) = 0.99, and it falsely flags 5% of healthy people, so P(+|not D) = 0.05. You test positive. What's the chance you actually have it? The numerator is 0.99 times 0.001, which is 0.00099. The denominator adds the false positives: 0.05 times 0.999, which is about 0.04995. So P(D|+) = 0.00099 / 0.05094, roughly 0.019, or about 2%. A positive result on a 99% accurate test still means only a 2% chance you're sick, because the disease is so rare that false positives swamp the true ones.

The mistake people make most often is the base rate fallacy: they confuse P(+|D), the test's accuracy, with P(D|+), the chance you're actually sick, and ignore how rare the condition is. That's why the prior P(D) matters so much, and why a second independent test on the same person can flip that 2% into something high.

items.question: Classic prisoner's dilemma. Each prisoner does better by confessing no matter what the other one does, so they both confess, even though both staying quiet would leave them better off.
items.answer: That's the core of it. Confessing is the **dominant strategy**: whatever the other prisoner does, you get a lighter sentence by confessing than by staying quiet. So rational self-interest drives both to confess, and they land on a worse outcome than if they'd both stayed silent. The tension is that the individually rational choice produces a collectively worse result, which is why it's a dilemma rather than just a bad decision.

items.question: what did he say about the second law earlier, and how does it connect to this?
items.answer: The second law says entropy in an isolated system never decreases, so heat flows from hot to cold on its own, never the reverse. That's why it sets the arrow of time: reversible processes keep entropy constant, irreversible ones raise it. The connection to what we're doing now is that any real cycle has losses, so efficiency is always below the ideal, and the entropy rise is exactly where that lost work goes.

items.question: But a lot of historians now call that the Westphalian myth. If you actually read the treaties, they say surprisingly little about sovereignty.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): So the Peace of Westphalia, 1648, ends the Thirty Years' War, and it's usually taught as the moment the modern system of sovereign states is born.

NATIVELY: The Peace of Westphalia is actually a pair of treaties signed in Münster and Osnabrück, and what it did was end the Thirty Years' War and settle the overlapping religious and dynastic conflicts that had torn apart the Holy Roman Empire. The "birth of the sovereign state" reading comes from the idea that it recognized each prince's authority over religion and territory within his own lands, which later got read back as the principle of non-interference in a state's internal affairs. Historians push back on that, though, because the settlement still left the Empire's structure and the emperor's role intact, so it's less a clean founding moment than a step in a longer shift toward territorial sovereignty.
items.answer: Right, and that's the revisionist reading in a nutshell. The treaties are mostly about concrete grievances: which princes could practice which faith, who got which territory, how the Empire's courts and diets would work. Sovereignty in the abstract barely appears. The "Westphalian" label is largely a twentieth-century back-projection, and the myth label sticks because the settlement preserved the Empire's layered authority rather than replacing it with a clean system of independent states.

items.question: So, can anyone tell me why the sky is blue but sunsets are red? Anybody? Think about wavelength, and think about how much air the light has to go through.
items.answer: Sunlight contains all colors, but the short blue wavelengths scatter far more in air than the long red ones, so blue gets bounced around the whole sky and reaches your eyes from every direction. At sunset the light travels through much more atmosphere, and most of the blue is scattered away before it gets to you, leaving the reds and oranges to come straight through.

items.question: Quick check before we move on. If I give you a heap with twelve keys, what's its height? Use our convention, not the book's.
items.answer: With our convention, height counts nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a heap with n keys has height floor(log2 n) + 1. For n = 12, floor(log2 12) is 3, so the height is **4**.
